name: Intense pulsed light (IPL photofacial)

lead: An IPL photofacial fires broad-spectrum light into the skin to fade sun spots, redness and small visible vessels, leaving a clearer, more even complexion. The same technology is used in some hair-removal systems.

A xenon lamp emits light of roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres. Filters remove most ultraviolet and long infrared light, and the rest is absorbed by melanin, haemoglobin and water, heating the targets. IPL was first developed for vascular conditions, and it is better documented for vascular lesions and hair reduction than for facial uses.

paras: People book a series of sessions at a clinic, where a practitioner picks a filter for the target, such as pigment or redness. Interchangeable filters let one device address different concerns, and sessions are usually spaced weeks apart.

Reported complications include temporary side effects and hyperpigmentation. Photosensitising medicines and skin damage are listed as contraindications, and IPL has been reported to worsen melasma. Rules for devices and operators vary by jurisdiction.

angle.text: IPL photofacials use pulses of broad-spectrum light absorbed by pigment and blood vessels, fading sun spots, redness and thread veins for a more even complexion. It is an established clinic technology with tunable filters; home devices are mostly sold for hair removal.

lead: Intense pulsed light (IPL) is a skin-treatment technology in which a computer-controlled xenon flashlamp emits pulses of broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1,200 nanometres, through filters that remove much ultraviolet and long infrared light. Unlike single-wavelength lasers, it can be tuned for different targets using interchangeable filters.

People use the cosmetic version, called a photofacial or photorejuvenation, to even out skin tone: the light is absorbed by brown pigment and by blood in small vessels, so sun spots, freckle-like marks, redness and thread veins fade and the face looks clearer and more uniform. IPL was first developed for vascular conditions and is also used for hair removal, rosacea, acne and dry-eye disease linked to meibomian gland dysfunction.

Systematic reviews report IPL among the options for solar lentigines, rosacea redness and hair removal [1][2][3]. Melasma is a special case, where light devices have shown benefit but recurrence is high, and a separate reference notes IPL may worsen it [4][5].
infobox: Vascular lesions 1995, pigmented lesions 1996, hair removal 1997

paras: Light pulses are absorbed by chromophores, mainly melanin, haemoglobin and water, which heat and are damaged. Pigmented spots absorb melanin-targeted wavelengths, and vessels absorb haemoglobin-targeted wavelengths.

Shimon Eckhouse invented IPL in 1992 and filed the detailed patent granted in 1995. ESC Medical commercialised it, and FDA clearances followed for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.

A 2025 systematic review of 41 trials in 3,234 patients with solar lentigines reported IPL success rates of 74.6 to 90 percent, compared with 27 to 57 percent for pulsed dye laser and 36 to 77 percent for Q-switched laser in the included studies [1]. Photorejuvenation also targets thread veins, photoaging and actinic keratosis.
A review of rosacea management says light therapies including IPL and pulsed dye laser are best used for the erythemato-telangiectatic type, in which redness and visible vessels dominate [2].

A 2013 review concluded the literature supports alexandrite, diode, Nd:YAG and IPL devices for long-term hair removal, noted the Nd:YAG is best for pigmented skin, and called for more research on home-use devices [3]. A 2006 comparison cited by Wikipedia found no significant difference in six-month hair reduction between alexandrite laser (68.75 percent), diode laser (71.71 percent) and IPL (66.96 percent).

A trial in 47 patients compared three IPL sessions with nightly benzoyl peroxide gel for inflammatory facial acne [6]. In eye care, a randomized study found IPL plus meibomian gland expression improved dry-eye measures in meibomian gland dysfunction [7], and another randomized study examined IPL for ocular demodicosis [8].

A 2022 systematic review reported that laser and light devices have been beneficial for melasma but recurrence remained high and combination therapies gave the best results [4]. Wikipedia's melasma page notes IPL may worsen it [5].

Hyperpigmentation is the main complication noted. Photosensitising medicines and damaged skin are listed as contraindications, and one manufacturer says its device suits light to medium skin tones. Longer-wavelength Nd:YAG lasers are preferred for pigmented skin in hair removal [3]. Regulation varies by jurisdiction, and a loose split between beauty-grade and medical-grade devices exists, including home hair-removal devices.

Human studies include the solar lentigines systematic review [1], randomized trials in meibomian gland dysfunction [7] and ocular demodicosis [8], a clinical trial against benzoyl peroxide in acne [6], and reviews of hair removal [3] and rosacea [2]. A 2006 comparison of hair-removal devices reported side effects of 9.5, 28.9 and 15.3 percent for alexandrite, diode and IPL, all temporary.
